findings.claim: The registry declares `reader.ReadOnlyCatalogReader.bundle` claim-level with `byte_level: False` and the semantics 'CLAIM-level, same rule as resolve_handle, plus SourceBundle assembly', and the module docstring states as MEASURED that both entry points 'verify the catalog's claim, never the bytes'. For `bundle` this is false: its bundle assembly opens and hashes artifact files, so its result depends on bytes.
findings.evidence: MY OWN OBSERVATION. Code: reader.py:353-389 builds the source dict from the catalog row/claim, then calls source_bundle.build_source_bundle (source_bundle.py:126) -> artifact_handle.validate_artifact, which does `path.is_file()` (artifact_handle.py:106) and `hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest()` (artifact_handle.py:111). Measurement (%TEMP%\b10vr\bundle_bytes.py, a ReadOnlyCatalogReader built with __new__ and three stubbed query methods over a temp artifact file, so no catalog is opened): with an intact artifact the instrumented counters recorded `is_file:normalized.md` and `read_bytes:normalized.md`, verdict reusable=['normalized']; after overwriting the file with different bytes the SAME call returned reusable=[] with reason='artifact_hash_mismatch' - a claim-level function could not notice. The gate's guard (test_b10_claim_level_adapters_never_read_bytes) passes because it only looks for the NAMES open/read_bytes/read_text/read_verified_bytes inside reader.py's own function bodies, so it cannot see filesystem access reached through a callee. resolve_handle is genuinely claim-level (verified the same way: no filesystem access at all).
findings.impact: A machine-readable registry entry - the deliverable of B10-1/B10-4 - states a factually wrong byte_level, and the guard that exists to protect it is name-local, so the same class of change made transitively (e.g. resolve_handle delegating to a helper that opens a file) would also pass. The 'switch stop' DECISION for bundle (keep it as an explicit adapter) is still the right call, but its recorded reason is wrong: bundle is claim-level on the SOURCE sha and byte-level on the ARTIFACTS. Anyone who trusts the registry will mis-describe the failure semantics - the exact thing B10-4 was supposed to pin down.
findings.suggested_disposition: Fix the entry to `byte_level: True` with an explicit split semantics ('claim-level on the source sha256; verifies each artifact's bytes through build_source_bundle/validate_artifact, so it can reject a bundle for artifact_hash_mismatch'), correct the module docstring's 'never the bytes' sentence for bundle, and consider making the claim-level guard walk the callee closure (or assert that the registered entry's transitive closure contains no read_bytes/open) instead of only the entry's own body.

findings.claim: CONFIRMED_DIRECT_READERS is documented as 'the ratchet baseline of places that still parse the shared documents.metadata_json column', and b10-recon.md section 1 labels the same list 'shared column documents.metadata_json'. The scan keys on the bare string 'metadata_json', and the schema has THREE same-named columns (documents / artifacts / locations), so the scan cannot tell them apart.
findings.evidence: MY OWN TABLE RESOLUTION (%TEMP%\b10vr\sqlctx.py over the reviewed revision, plus a read of each feeding query). artifacts.metadata_json: artifact_backfill.py::_classify (row is an artifact row; the site's own comment at :177 says 'the artifacts table has no such columns'); artifact_read_model.py::_artifact_row (SQL 'FROM artifacts WHERE artifact_id=?'); section_query.py::SectionQueryService (SQL 'SELECT a.document_id, a.path, a.metadata_json ... FROM artifacts a JOIN documents d'); normalizer.py::normalize_catalog's SECOND site (document['normalization_metadata_json'] <- 'existing.metadata_json AS normalization_metadata_json', 'LEFT JOIN artifacts existing'). documents.metadata_json: normalizer.py::_frontmatter; normalizer.py::normalize_catalog's FIRST site (document['metadata_json'] from 'SELECT d.* ... FROM documents d JOIN sources s'); resolver.py::_metadata_conflict_reason ('SELECT metadata_json FROM documents'); scanner.py::_merge_document_row ('SELECT ... metadata_json ... FROM documents'); service.py::SourceCatalog ('entity_rows = ... SELECT d.metadata_json ... FROM documents d', consumed at service.py:434 - I initially mis-attributed this one to the locations row that a LATER query (service.py:404-415) builds, and corrected it after reading the loop at service.py:417); source_lifecycle.py::_safety_receipt ('SELECT metadata_json FROM documents'). Net: 3 of the 9 baselined keys are wholly artifact-column readers, 1 reads BOTH columns (one site each), and 5 are documents-column readers. A third same-named column (locations.metadata_json, selected at service.py:408) is not in the baseline today but would be caught by the same string match. The conflation also appears in read_chain.HEURISTIC_READER_CANDIDATES (extraction_quality, prompt_injection*) and in b10-plan.md section 1's list ('仍在自行解析共享列 documents.metadata_json 的模块: artifact_backfill.py:175, artifact_read_model.py:105, extraction_quality.py:195, ...').
findings.impact: B10-3's convergence work list is mis-scoped: converging an artifacts-column reader onto store.metadata_object 'because it reads the shared documents column' is a different change from what the registry says, and lowering the baseline by doing so would be recorded as progress on the documents chain. It also produces a false-positive gate error message for genuinely different columns (finding B-VR-B10-05). No data-safety impact: metadata_object is behaviourally identical, so converging them is harmless - the defect is in what the artifact CLAIMS to measure.
findings.suggested_disposition: Resolve (table, column) per site from the feeding SQL (or from the row's provenance) and either key the baseline as 'artifacts.metadata_json::symbol' / 'documents.metadata_json::symbol' or rename the registry to 'metadata_json parse sites across the catalog schema' and split the ratchet into one baseline per table. Re-run the inventory after the change and correct the recon/plan wording.

findings.claim: The convergence ratchet is bypassable: 8 constructed shapes that add a NEW direct reader of the column pass the entire gate (7 passed each time), while the 2 positive controls are correctly killed. The gate is a ratchet over one common shape, not a proof that no new direct reader appeared.
findings.evidence: MY OWN CONSTRUCTION AND RUN (%TEMP%\b10vr\run_mutations.py, each case applied to a pristine temp copy of c4a69e0; results in vr_mutations.json). ALLOWED (gate green): VR-B1 aliased FUNCTION import; VR-B2 parse-by-helper; VR-B3 json.JSONDecoder().decode; VR-B4 rename-the-value-then-loads (lands in the unenforced heuristic list); VR-B5 a new method inside the already-baselined class SourceCatalog (key collapses to `service.py::SourceCatalog`); VR-B6 a reader outside the scanned root; VR-B10 getattr(json,'loads')(...); VR-B11 a concatenated key. BLOCKED (gate red): VR-P1 `import json as j; j.loads(...)`, VR-P2 `row.get('metadata_json')`. The registry itself notes that the first version of the baseline was written from memory and that the heuristic list is 'reported, never enforced', so the boundary is partly acknowledged - but no document in the reviewed increment states that a new reader can enter without tripping the ratchet, and the gate's own failure text presents the baseline as the thing that 'may only shrink'.
findings.impact: A future contributor (or the same author in B10-3) can add a real second read chain - most plausibly by renaming the value in a new function (VR-B4) or by adding a method to SourceCatalog (VR-B5) - and the contract suite stays green, so 'the read chain stays single' is not enforced for those shapes. The class-key variant also defeats the author's uncommitted COLUMN_VALUE_HANDOFFS ratchet, whose baseline contains the same class names.
findings.suggested_disposition: State the measured boundary in read_chain.py (the author's uncommitted text already does this for the helper shape) and harden the scan: (a) detect any call that RECEIVES a subscript/.get() of the column (the uncommitted second ratchet), (b) key by (file, symbol, line-range) or by SITE COUNT per symbol so a second reader inside an existing key is visible, (c) match the exact key `metadata_json` instead of the substring, (d) treat `from json import loads [as X]` as the same callee. None of these is a completeness proof either - the honest claim is 'a ratchet over the shapes we can see'.

findings.claim: At least one REAL reader of the shared documents.metadata_json column is in NEITHER registry tuple and cannot be found by the gate: scanner.py::_previous_provenance_fields. The registry therefore under-reports the sites that B10-3 still has to converge.
findings.evidence: MY OWN SCAN + CODE READ. scanner.py:1405 `stored = json.loads(stored_json or "{}")` inside `_previous_provenance_fields(stored_json)`, called at scanner.py:1739 as `_previous_provenance_fields(existing_document["metadata_json"])` where existing_document came from `SELECT ... metadata_json ... FROM documents` (scanner.py:1006-1010). The heuristic rule requires the enclosing symbol to mention the column, and this helper's body never does; the call site's callee is not `loads`. Confirmed by my scanner: the site does not appear in either set under either attribution convention. The author's manual plan list DOES name scanner.py:1405, so the machine-derived registry dropped a site that was already known. Same mechanism hides extraction_quality.py::_artifact_metadata (artifacts column, json.loads at :195 via `_artifact_metadata(row["metadata_json"])` at :373).
findings.impact: Under-reporting is the dangerous direction: the confirmed baseline is the only enforced list, and it is neither complete for 'documents.metadata_json' (this site) nor narrowly scoped to it (4 sites of other tables, finding B-VR-B10-02). A reviewer applying the recorded rule 'the 9 confirmed sites remain to be converged' would miss this one.
findings.suggested_disposition: Add the call-site-based handoff scan (the author's uncommitted COLUMN_VALUE_HANDOFFS does catch both of these: they are in its 12-entry baseline) and say explicitly in read_chain.py which list is the convergence work list.

findings.claim: The gate produces a FALSE POSITIVE on a legitimate new module that parses a differently-named column of another table, because it matches the substring 'metadata_json' anywhere in the call's argument.
findings.evidence: MY OWN CONSTRUCTION AND RUN: a new module with `json.loads(row["acquisition_metadata_json"] or "{}")` makes test_b10_no_new_confirmed_direct_reader FAIL with the message 'new direct readers of the shared column: ... - converge them onto store.metadata_object, or register and justify them in read_chain.CONFIRMED_DIRECT_READERS'. That column is not documents.metadata_json. The naming pattern is idiomatic in this codebase (`normalization_metadata_json` already exists and is baselined).
findings.impact: In normal development the gate demands either a wrong convergence (re-pointing a different column's reader at the documents chain) or an unjustified baseline entry, and it teaches contributors that the baseline is a list of 'shared column readers' when it is a list of name matches. Compounds B-VR-B10-02.
findings.suggested_disposition: Match the exact subscript/.get() key (the author's uncommitted handoff scan already does this) and only count calls whose argument reads the column as a VALUE.

findings.claim: The claim that the two metadata readers were 'the SAME contract' with 'equivalent catch sets' is not exactly true: the delegated chain catches a STRICTLY NARROWER set of exceptions than the adapter did, and the equivalence claim has no evidence artifact in RUN.
findings.evidence: MY OWN MEASUREMENT. Old (b829b03~1 service.py:92-96): `except (TypeError, ValueError, RecursionError)`. New (store.metadata_object, store.py:946-950): `except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError, RecursionError, UnicodeDecodeError)` - every one of those is a subclass of the old set, so the new set is a subset. Consequence, measured: an object whose __bool__ raises a bare ValueError returns {} through the old adapter and RAISES ValueError through the new one (input_sha16 de9bfc5ec6dde690). The reverse direction cannot happen. All the shapes the record names (None/''/'{}'/'[]'/invalid JSON/'123'/dict/deep-nesting RecursionError/non-UTF-8 bytes, 22 of my 24 inputs) are identical. Reachability: the only call site (service.py:736) passes `document["metadata_json"]`, a sqlite TEXT value (store._tolerate_undecodable_text makes it a str), so the divergence is not reachable in production today. The docstring/commit text asserts 'their catch sets are equivalent ... both return {} for anything that is not a JSON object', and there is no script or log for the '8 pathological inputs' in RUN (I re-measured them myself).
findings.impact: The converged adapter's guarantee is now slightly narrower than the one it replaced, which is a real (if currently unreachable) contract change recorded as if it were a pure equivalence. If a future caller passes a non-str/bytes object with a raising __bool__/read, the old name would have returned {} and the new one raises - and SourceCatalog.query has no guard around that call.
findings.suggested_disposition: Write the direction precisely ('the chain's catch set is a subset of the adapter's; JSONDecodeError/UnicodeDecodeError are ValueError subclasses') and either record the 8-input matrix as an evidence file or state that it was measured without an artifact to publish.

findings.claim: 'repository_untouched=true' is scoped to src/**/*.py, and the recorded fingerprint value is not reproducible from git, so the claim is a self-consistency check rather than a re-derivable fact.
findings.evidence: b10_mutations.py::_repo_fingerprint hashes `(repo/'src').rglob('*.py')` as 'relpath size sha256' and returns hexdigest()[:16]; tests/, scripts/ and root files are outside it (the record's section 4 wording does say 'src/**/*.py', so the scope is disclosed - the JSON KEY 'repository_untouched' is what overstates). I recomputed the same construction: my git-archive copy of the reviewed revision fingerprints c2580ba5abbeee27 and the live tree af7163024566828f, neither equal to the recorded 5202ca372c6929ea; the value depends on the working tree's mixed LF/CRLF checkout state (git archive gave my copy CRLF for all files while the live tree is mixed), so it is environment-dependent by construction. Before==after within one run is still a valid check, and the harness only ever writes inside its own temp copy, so I found no evidence of any repository write.
findings.impact: A future reader cannot verify the recorded number, and 'repository_untouched' as a name suggests a scope wider than what was hashed. Low risk in practice (the tool's write path is temp-only).
findings.suggested_disposition: Rename the field to src_py_fingerprint_unchanged, and/or fingerprint the bytes git would report (blob hashes via `git status --porcelain` / `git diff --stat` being empty) so the value is re-derivable.

adjudication_reason: No live P0. The product change itself - service._read_shared_metadata delegating to store.metadata_object - is behaviourally equivalent on every input reachable from its only call site (22 of my 24 inputs identical, including the deep-nesting RecursionError path, non-object JSON, non-UTF-8 bytes and None/''/'{}'/'[]'/invalid/'123'/dict; the single divergence needs a non-str object whose __bool__ raises a bare ValueError, which the sqlite TEXT column cannot produce). The gate works for what it claims to measure: I independently reproduced the adapters/ hole with the pre-fix test file and its closure with the reviewed one, killed all five of my own mutants by assertion on the expected tests, reproduced the author's committed 7/7 mutation proof by re-running the committed harness on the reviewed revision, and confirmed the '7 passed' baseline on a clean copy. Converging a site onto the chain is explicitly not punished. What keeps this from a clean APPROVE is the registry itself: one of its three entries (reader.bundle) is declared byte_level False / 'never opens a file' while it demonstrably reads and hashes artifact bytes and changes its verdict when they change (P1), the ratchet baseline conflates three same-named columns while claiming to be the documents.metadata_json list (P2), and the ratchet is bypassable by at least seven constructed shapes including the two most natural ones (P2). None of those makes the increment unsafe to keep; all of them mean the increment's central artifact - the machine-readable registry - currently says things about the code that are not true, which is exactly what a later convergence batch (B10-3) will rely on. The three P2/P1 items should be fixed (or the boundary stated in the registry) before the next convergence batch is planned from this list.
